newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador city charred and stunned by U.S. jet crash.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador city charred and stunned by U.S. jet crash.

text.p: The poor neighbourhood of the Ecuadoran city of Manta that became a hell of burning jet fuel and wreckage after it was hit by a U.S.-owned Boeing 707 has a tragically apt name: Dolorosa, Spanish for "painful".
Manta, a port on the Pacific coast 290 miles (480 km) southeast of Quito, was about to celebrate a local fiesta.

Instead the stench of burning wreckage hung over blackened ruins in the working-class barrio of Dolorosa on Wednesday as its shocked residents searched for friends and relatives and counted their casualties: 22 dead and 60 injured.

"Families here still can't believe what happened. They're searching desperately for those missing... People are crying. One lady just fainted from anxiety after finding her loved one," local Red Cross chief Javier Reyes told Reuters.

The Millon Air freight plane, bound for Miami with flowers and frozen fish, caught fire just after take-off and ploughed into the densely-populated city-centre neighorhood at 10:40 p.m. local time on Tuesday (0340 GMT on Wednesday).
Rescuers had to wait for daybreak because the crashing plane took out electricity lines as it rained fire and death on eight blocks of Dolorosa, four of which were reduced to rubble, rescuers said.
The crew of three Americans and a Colombian died, but most of the victims were on the ground, many of them burnt to death by the estimated 14,000 gallons of fuel on board.

"All of Manta was wrapped in flames because of the fuel," one witness, Miguel Narea Zea, told Reuters. "It was like a bomb going off, like being in a war. I live three blocks from the accident site and just grabbed all my loved ones."
Some bodies were so badly burnt they could not be counted, let alone identified, said Roman Catholic Bishop Mario Ruiz.
"We can't get a clear picture of the tragedy because there are charred bodies," he said.

The bishop's voice faltered as he said the first victim was Padre Gabriel, the parish priest into whose church was directly hit by the burning wreck of the Boeing 707: "The plane crashed straight into his room."
But Padre Gabriel's church may have shielded some of the humble houses around it from even worse damage.
"The tragedy would have been much worse if the church had not taken the impact. It would have hit houses made of bricks and wood," said another unidentified eye-witness.
"One wing hit a building by the church and as the wings are where the fuel is kept, it exploded in a sheet of flames, just like the movies, and three people were burnt," he said.
Hospitals in the fishing town pleaded for fresh blood, medicine and burn ointment and the city morgue housed a pile of charred corpses in body bags awaiting identification.

"We have declared three days of mourning in the city of Manta to show solidiarity with the families affected," said Jorge Zambrano, mayor of the city hit by the worst air tragedy in Ecuador in a decade.
National police chief Marco Hinojosa ordered special patrols in Dolorosa "to stop criminals from using it as an excuse for looting."
